A grep for `signal_generate`/`sys_enter_kill`/`tp/signal` handlers in bpftools returned nothing, so no parallel signal stream exists that could let a downstream consumer recover the fatal-signal status. The only caveat softening the impact prose (not the defect) is that `grep -rn '\.exit_code'` shows no current blame/attribution or crash-detection logic keying on the value — it is stored and displayed, not yet consumed for decisions — so this is a real semantic/data-correctness defect that will poison the planned experiment and reporting layer rather than a currently-active logic bug. The proposed fix (branch on raw value; emit status when `raw > 0xff`, else the signal number with a signaled flag) matches the standard bcc `exitsnoop` idiom and is correct.

confirmed.title: Every SSL event reserves the full 256 KiB record, contradicting the documented header+payload reserve
confirmed.evidence: SSL_exit and ex_SSL_exit both call bpf_ringbuf_reserve(&rb, sizeof(*data), 0) (lines 147 and 278), and struct probe_SSL_data_t embeds __u8 buf[MAX_BUF_SIZE] with MAX_BUF_SIZE = 256*1024 (tls_capture.h:35), so the reservation is ~262 KB regardless of payload. tls_capture.h:31-34 and tests/test_tls_capture_header.c:8-10,86-94 claim the program reserves 'the header plus the bytes it actually copies'; RING_BUFFER_SIZE is 64 MiB (tls_capture.h:15), which yields only ~255 in-flight records.
confirmed.impact: Every short SSL_read/SSL_write (HTTP/2 frames, SSE chunks, small tool responses) consumes 256 KiB of ring space. A few hundred queued events exhaust the ring, so bursts drop payloads (the counter records them, but the data is gone from GT/session evidence), and the documented reservation contract is not what the code does.
confirmed.fix: Select among a few compile-time-constant reservation sizes based on payload length (e.g. header-only, 4 KiB, 64 KiB, 256 KiB) so the verifier still sees a constant per branch; size the ring from the expected event mix and update the header/test contract to match.

verification.reason: The claim's code facts check out exactly. In /tmp/mtal-audit/bpftools/tls_capture/tls_capture.bpf.c, `SSL_exit` computes `u32 buf_copy_size = min((size_t)MAX_BUF_SIZE, (size_t)len)` at line 146 but then calls `bpf_ringbuf_reserve(&rb, sizeof(*data), 0)` at line 147, and `ex_SSL_exit` does the same at line 278 after clamping `buf_copy_size` at lines 269-272. Since `struct probe_SSL_data_t` embeds `__u8 buf[MAX_BUF_SIZE]` as its last member with `MAX_BUF_SIZE (256 * 1024)` (tls_capture.h:12, 35), every read/write exit event reserves ~262 KB regardless of the actual payload. The only exception is the `do_handshake` uretprobe, which correctly reserves `__builtin_offsetof(struct probe_SSL_data_t, buf)` at lines 402-403 — so the title's "every SSL event" is marginally overbroad, but the two payload-bearing program paths (attached via SEC("uretprobe/SSL_read") at line 187 and SEC("uretprobe/SSL_read_ex") at line 337, wired up through attach_openssl at tls_capture.c:408-436) are precisely as claimed, and there is no other mitigation: the rb map's only sizing source is `RING_BUFFER_SIZE` (tls_capture.bpf.c:15) and ring_buffer__new (tls_capture.c:712) does not enlarge it. The documented contract in tls_capture.h:31-34 and tests/test_tls_capture_header.c:8-10,88 ("reserves only the header plus the bytes it actually copies") is stale and contradicted by the code, while the header comment at lines 12-14 and the test assertion at test_tls_capture_header.c:94-95 ("ring holds >=200 full-size records (constant reserve)") already acknowledge the constant full-record reserve. With 64 MiB and ~262,216-byte records, at most ~255 records can be in flight (fewer once ringbuf's per-record 8-byte header and page-boundary padding are counted), so a burst of a few hundred small HTTP/2/SSE events exhausts the ring and payload evidence is lost even though inc_dropped() records it. Nothing in the code refutes the claim; only the handshake-path detail narrows its scope.

confirmed.title: BoringSSL fallback attaches handshake probes at file offset 0 when the handshake pattern was not found
confirmed.evidence: find_boringssl_offsets sets result.found = true even when ssl_do_handshake remains 0 (lines 280-293, 323) — the code and test explicitly allow this for Bun >= v1.4. attach_openssl_by_offset then gates the handshake probes only on env.handshake, not on offsets->ssl_do_handshake != 0 (lines 468-473), so with --handshake it calls bpf_program__attach_uprobe_opts with offset 0. __CHECK_PROGRAM only tests that the link is non-NULL.
confirmed.impact: The uprobes are installed on the ELF header, which is never executed. The run produces no handshake events and reports no error, so a missing handshake is indistinguishable from a binary that never handshakes. This is the exact configuration the code documents as expected on current Bun builds.
confirmed.fix: Skip the handshake attach when offsets->ssl_do_handshake == 0 and log why; return per-function validity from find_boringssl_offsets instead of a single found flag.

verification.reason: The claim survives every refutation attempt. In /tmp/mtal-audit/bpftools/tls_capture/tls_capture.c, find_boringssl_offsets initializes `result` to zero and only ever sets `result.ssl_do_handshake` inside the delta check (line 277) or the independent pattern search (line 291); when neither matches it merely logs a verbose-only message (line 289) and falls through to an unconditional `result.found = true` at line 323. So `ssl_do_handshake == 0` is an unambiguous "not found" sentinel, and the test at bpftools/tests/test_tls_capture_boringssl_offsets.c:57-62 explicitly blesses that state as normal for Bun >= v1.4. The caller checks only `offsets.found` (line 702) and then calls attach_openssl_by_offset, which gates the handshake probes solely on `env.handshake` (lines 468-473) and passes `offsets->ssl_do_handshake` straight through as the file offset. The offset-attach macros (lines 101-117) set no `func_name`, so libbpf treats the value as a raw file offset, and __CHECK_PROGRAM (lines 55-61) only tests that the returned link is non-NULL — perf_event_open/uprobe registration does not validate that the file offset lands in an executable segment, so a zero offset yields a successfully-created but dead link (or one that is never applied to any vma), with no events and no error. The return value of attach_openssl_by_offset is also ignored at line 704, and the only diagnostic about the missing pattern is hidden behind `verbose`. The test file confirms rather than refutes the premise: detection is expected to report found=true with handshake offset 0 on current Bun builds, which is exactly the configuration that reaches this attach path. I found no other validation of ssl_do_handshake anywhere before attachment (grep of lines 180-340 and 440-720 shows none).

confirmed.title: Entry-map failures and return-probe state misses drop TLS events without touching dropped_events
confirmed.evidence: The entry probes ignore bpf_map_update_elem failures (lines 104-106, 209-213, 230-234), and the return probes return 0 without inc_dropped() when bufs/start_ns/readbytes_ptrs lookups fail (lines 124-125, 253-254, 323-325, 340-342). The same pattern exists in stdiocap.bpf.c: enter_common ignores the map update at line 75, and exit_common returns silently on a failed lookup at lines 89-91. inc_dropped() is only called for ringbuf reserve failures.
confirmed.impact: When the per-thread state maps are full or an update fails, payload events vanish while TLS_RINGBUF_STATS/RINGBUF_STATS still report a low or zero drop count. Capture-health checks that rely on those counters can certify an incomplete capture.
confirmed.fix: Check every bpf_map_update_elem return and call inc_dropped() on failure; count return-probe state misses (a separate counter is useful to distinguish ring pressure from state loss); apply the same accounting in stdiocap.

verification.reason: The cited behavior is present exactly as claimed. In /tmp/mtal-audit/bpftools/tls_capture/tls_capture.bpf.c, inc_dropped() (lines 84-91) is invoked only at ringbuf-reserve failure sites (149, 280, 405). All four entry probes discard the return value of bpf_map_update_elem: probe_SSL_rw_enter at 104-106, probe_SSL_write_ex_enter at 209-213 (plus 212 readbytes_ptrs), and probe_SSL_read_ex_enter at 230-234. The return paths then silently return 0 on state misses: SSL_exit on bufs lookup 123-125 and start_ns 127-129; ex_SSL_exit on bufs 252-254 and start_ns 256-258; and the _ex return probes on readbytes_ptrs lookup at 323-325 and 341-343 (the claim's 340-342 is off by one/two lines but denotes the same early `if (!readbytes_ptr) return 0;`). Notably the ssls lookup is treated as optional (sslp ? *sslp : 0 at 176/293), so its loss does not drop an event, and the claim does not overstate that part. stdiocap.bpf.c matches too: enter_common ignores the io_args update at line 75, and exit_common's bpf_map_lookup_elem at 89-91 returns 0 without inc_dropped(), which is called only at the ringbuf-reserve failure on line 100. I also confirmed the impact path rather than trusting it: tls_capture.c emits RINGBUF_STATS/TLS_RINGBUF_STATS from dropped_events only (lines 730-756), and compare/scripts/build/build_backend_capture_health.py requires tls_drop_count == 0 (lines 133-135, 147-164, 180-182), while compare/scripts/audit/audit_paper_experiment_readiness.py (lines 967-976) treats any nonzero drop/loss counter as a blocking problem. Thus a filled per-tid state map (e.g., leaked entries from missed uretprobes or many threads) or a failed update causes payload events to disappear while the health artifact still certifies zero drops. No other counter or userspace compensation for entry-failure/return-miss exists, so the claim cannot be refuted; medium severity is appropriate since it requires map pressure rather than occurring on every capture.

confirmed.title: Kernel file-open noise filter is over-broad, uncounted, and also suppresses destructive mutations
confirmed.evidence: is_file_open_noise drops any path beginning with /sys, /proc, /dev, /lib (lines 50-63) or /usr/lib, /usr/share (lines 65-72) with no path-separator boundary, so /system..., /devops..., /library... are also dropped. It is applied to open/openat and to unlink/unlinkat/rmdir/truncate/rename (lines 296, 358, 417, 501) and never increments any counter. Only ringbuf reserve failures increment dropped_events (lines 33-40).
confirmed.impact: A zero dropped_events count does not mean complete observation: an uncounted, over-broad class of opens is removed before the ring buffer, and destructive actions in filtered trees (for example unlink of /dev/shm files or /usr/share data) never become FILE_DELETE/FILE_TRUNCATE/FILE_RENAME events. GT action traces and FPR/TPR denominators are silently biased.
confirmed.fix: Match prefixes with a trailing '/', apply the noise filter only to FILE_OPEN (not mutations), and expose a filtered_events counter per category alongside dropped_events so consumers can account for the excluded volume.

verification.reason: Re-reading /tmp/mtal-audit/bpftools/process/process.bpf.c confirms every element of the claim. is_file_open_noise (lines 47-81) compares raw characters with no path-separator boundary: line 50 matches "/sys" so "/system..." and any "/sysX" path is dropped; line 54 matches "/proc..."; line 58 matches "/dev..." so "/devops..." and "/dev/shm/..." are dropped; line 62 matches "/lib..." so "/library..." is dropped; lines 65-72 match "/usr/lib*" and "/usr/sha*" (only filepath[4]=='/' is required, chars 5-7 are unprefixed), so "/usr/libfoo" and "/usr/sharedata" are also dropped. The filter is invoked at line 296 (trace_openat), line 358 (trace_open), line 417 (trace_mutation, reached from trace_unlinkat line 456, trace_unlink line 465, trace_rmdir line 472, trace_truncate line 479) and line 501 (trace_rename_paths, reached from trace_renameat2 line 538, trace_renameat line 547, trace_rename line 554), each with a bare `return 0;` that never calls inc_dropped(). inc_dropped (lines 33-40) is only reachable from ringbuf-reserve failures at lines 116, 167, 250, 302, 364, 422, 506 and 631, so the consumer's PROCESS_RINGBUF_STATS "dropped_events" value (process.c lines 530-542) cannot reflect filtered volume; grep across bpftools/collector/compare found no filtered_events or equivalent counter. The impact also survives: userspace process.c lines 714-731 explicitly handles is_open and non-OPEN ops by calling print_file_event, so FILE_DELETE/FILE_TRUNCATE/FILE_RENAME are normally emitted — the only thing removing mutations under /dev, /proc, /sys, /lib, /usr/lib and /usr/share is this uncounted eBPF filter, meaning unlink/truncate/rename of e.g. /dev/shm or /usr/share data is silently absent while dropped_events still reads 0. The proposed boundary fix and separating OPEN-only filtering are sound; severity medium is appropriate (not critical because it does not corrupt emitted events, but it does bias completeness/denominator claims).

confirmed.title: openat/unlinkat/renameat discard dirfd, so relative paths cannot be resolved to a file
confirmed.evidence: trace_openat reads dirfd into dfd (lines 281, 287) but never stores or uses it; the event carries only the raw user pointer's string (line 324). trace_unlinkat ignores ctx->args[0] and uses only args[1] (line 456), and trace_renameat/renameat2 likewise drop both dirfd arguments (line 547).
confirmed.impact: openat(AT_FDCWD, "package.json") or openat(dirfd, "config") is recorded as the bare relative path. Two processes opening the same-named file in different directories collide in resource/action graphs, and the actual file touched cannot be reconstructed from the event — directly undermining file-resource provenance and attribution.
confirmed.fix: Carry dirfd (plus an AT_FDCWD marker) in the event and resolve it to a path in userspace via /proc/<pid>/fd/<dirfd> at emit time, or capture the process cwd at EXEC and resolve relative paths there; apply the same to unlinkat/renameat.

verification.reason: The cited code says exactly what the claim states and nothing compensates for it. In /tmp/mtal-audit/bpftools/process/process.bpf.c, trace_openat declares `int dfd, flags;` at line 281, assigns `dfd = (int)ctx->args[0];` at line 287, and never references dfd again — the event is populated at line 324 from the raw filename string only, and the struct in process.h:89-97 has no dirfd/cwd field to carry it. trace_unlinkat (line 456) forwards only ctx->args[1], and trace_renameat/trace_renameat2 (lines 547 and 540) forward only args[1]/args[3], discarding both dirfds. I searched for any userspace or BPF-side recovery and found none: no chdir/fchdir probe exists (grep over the tree hits only resolve_bash_path and test os.chdir), the sole /proc/<pid>/fd reader is process_ext/map_flush.h:66 which belongs to a different probe, and collector/src/framework/runners/process.rs:39-99 forwards the JSON verbatim. The noise filter is_file_open_noise (lines 47-81) matches only absolute prefixes like /sys, /proc, /dev, /lib, /usr, so relative paths are emitted unchanged rather than dropped. The consequence is real downstream, e.g. handoff_injection.rs:238-248 keys propagation state on filepath.to_string() and matches filepath.contains("/env/scenarios/fixtures/"), both of which fail for a bare relative name, and the process runner is genuinely wired in (binary_extractor.rs:55-56, doctor.rs:324), so this is not dead code. Severity medium is appropriate as a provenance/attribution gap rather than a crash.

confirmed.title: stdiocap resolves fd_target after the fact, so provenance can be missing or point at a reused fd
confirmed.evidence: print_event calls resolve_fd_target(event->pid, event->fd, ...) (line 192), which readlinks /proc/<pid>/fd/<fd> (lines 158-170) when the userspace consumer prints the event — after the syscall completed and possibly after the descriptor was closed or its number reused by another open.
confirmed.impact: fd_target is null for short-lived pipes/sockets (the common case for tool stdout) and can attribute a read/write to an unrelated file that later received the same fd number, producing false provenance in stdio evidence used for content-taint and GT review.
confirmed.fix: Capture the file identity in the probe at syscall time (inode/device or a path from struct file) instead of readlinking later; at minimum mark the late resolution as best-effort with a resolution timestamp so consumers do not treat it as authoritative.

verification.reason: The cited code says exactly what the claim states and nothing else resolves the fd earlier. In /tmp/mtal-audit/bpftools/stdiocap/stdiocap.c, resolve_fd_target() at lines 158-170 formats "/proc/%d/fd/%d" and calls readlink() against the target's current state, and print_event() invokes it at line 192; handle_event() (lines 229-237) calls print_event() for every ring-buffer record, so this is the normal path, not dead code. The BPF side proves no syscall-time identity is available to fall back on: io_args_t stores only buf/start_ns/fd/is_read (stdiocap.bpf.c lines 7-12), enter_common() records only the fd number (lines 61-77), exit_common() copies only event->fd (lines 105-113), and struct stdiocap_event_t (stdiocap.h lines 9-23) carries no inode, device, path, or timestamp for the resolution. The value is emitted as an ordinary authoritative-looking field; StdioRunner::parse_stdio_event passes the raw JSON through (collector/src/framework/runners/stdio.rs lines 91-122), and scripts/spikes/p3b-stdio-read-coverage.sh lines 120 and 162 gates coverage on `fd_target` containing the fixture path, so late resolution directly affects a real validation. Nothing downstream re-resolves or flags it, so the null-on-exit and fd-number-reuse TOCTOU are both reachable. Two qualifiers reduce but do not refute the impact: a live pipe or socket resolves to pipe:[inode]/socket:[inode] rather than null, so null is not literally "the common case for tool stdout" while the target lives; and main.rs (around line 1426) requires --pid, making the traced target normally long-lived. However, the --all-fds mode used by the p3b spike traces transient file descriptors that are commonly closed immediately after the read, and events still buffered when the target exits are printed only after /proc/<pid> is gone, so both missing and misattributed provenance are real. The proposed fix (capture file identity in the probe, or explicitly mark the value best-effort/with a resolution timestamp) is appropriate.

confirmed.title: Causal-enrichment fields and the process_ext aggregation path are dead wiring
confirmed.evidence: struct event declares pgid (line 74) and cgroup_id/uid/gid/seq_number/parent_uid/parent_cgroup_id (lines 79-84), but process.bpf.c never assigns any of them and process_json.h/process.c never emit them. enrichment.h is included by no translation unit; process_ext/map_flush.h and process_ext/mem_info.h plus process_new.h are referenced only by tests (Makefile:216-222, tests/test_process_map_flush.c:26-28, tests/test_process_mem_info.c:17, tests/test_process_header.c:28-29). The dormant path also keeps a second, non-equivalent JSON escaper (process_ext/map_flush.h:37-50) that does not escape control characters.
confirmed.impact: Every ring record carries roughly 40 bytes of never-written fields (reducing the effective 1 MiB ring occupancy), and the code advertises kernel-side causal enrichment that no producer fills. The collector already works around the missing fields by reading /proc at EXEC (collector/src/responsibility/runtime/routing.rs:560-580), so the declarations only create a false contract and maintenance surface.
confirmed.fix: Delete enrichment.h, process_ext/, process_new.h and their tests, and remove the unpopulated fields from struct event; if enrichment is wanted, implement it end-to-end (BPF write + JSON emit + consumer) rather than keeping declarations.

verification.reason: The cited code says exactly what the claim reports. In bpftools/process/process.h, `pgid` is declared at line 74 and the six enrichment fields at lines 79-84 (cgroup_id, uid, gid, seq_number, parent_uid, parent_cgroup_id); a repo-wide grep for each name in the snapshot finds no other occurrence in any .bpf.c, process.c, or process_json.h, so nothing assigns or emits them. All eight ring-buffer producers in process/process.bpf.c reserve `sizeof(*e)` (lines 114, 165, 248, 300, 362, 420, 504, 629) and initialize fields one by one (e.g. 120-138), so the declared-but-unwritten bytes (36 bytes of payload plus alignment padding, ~48 bytes of record growth rather than exactly 40) ride in every record and are not zeroed by bpf_ringbuf_reserve. process.c handle_event (594-700) and process_json.h print_file_event/print_network_event (33-60, 110+) never reference them. enrichment.h is included by no translation unit (grep for `enrichment.h` returns only the file itself and design docs), and process_ext/map_flush.h, process_ext/mem_info.h, and process/process_new.h are referenced only from Makefile:216-222 test rules and tests/test_process_map_flush.c:26-28, tests/test_process_mem_info.c:17, tests/test_process_header.c:28-29 — process_new.h:40-42 itself states the process_ext/ aggregation path "no BPF program in this repository is built from." The duplicate escaper is real: process_ext/map_flush.h:37-50 escapes only backslash, quote, \n and \t, leaving other control bytes raw, and bpftools/include/json_escape.h:8-9 documents that divergence explicitly. The workaround is also confirmed at collector/src/responsibility/runtime/routing.rs:558-571 (comment plus read_pgid/read_unit from /proc at EXEC), with matching acknowledgements in proc_stat.rs:13-14 and cgroup.rs:7. The only inaccuracy is "roughly 40 bytes" (the padding makes it about 48 bytes per event), which does not undermine the defect; low severity is appropriate, so no adjustment.

confirmed.title: ConnectionBuffer request reassembly is absent from the trace/record chain
confirmed.evidence: connection_buffer.rs:5-12 states that large request bodies span multiple SSL_write calls and must be reassembled; the analyzer is added only in run_raw_ssl (collector/src/main.rs:964-965). The production `record` command dispatches to run_trace (main.rs:708-742), whose SSL chain (main.rs:1373-1409) adds TimestampNormalizer, PayloadNormalizer, RawSecretRedactor, SSLFilter, SSEProcessor, HTTPParser, HTTPFilter and AuthHeaderRemover — never ConnectionBuffer. PayloadNormalizer buffers only READ/RECV (payload_normalizer.rs:104-120), so every WRITE/SEND fragment passes through untouched. docs/architecture.md:182 claims ConnectionBuffer applies to '全管道' (the whole pipeline).
confirmed.impact: In the record/trace product path every request body larger than one SSL_write is delivered as fragments: the first fragment (request line + headers + partial body) is parsed by HTTPParser as a complete request, and continuation fragments become opaque ssl events. Prompt/tool-call content in LLM requests is silently truncated, so intent extraction and injection detection are measured on incomplete inputs.
confirmed.fix: Insert ConnectionBuffer immediately after PayloadNormalizer and before SSLFilter in run_trace's SSL chain, flush its buffered requests and pending queue at EOF, and add an end-to-end request-split test mirroring collector/tests/response_chain.rs.

verification.reason: The claim survives re-reading. connection_buffer.rs:5-12 explicitly states SSL_write bodies span multiple eBPF calls and must be accumulated per connection; its Analyzer impl only emits the assembled request when a response-start/read event arrives (lines 152-190), and no other request assembler exists in the tree (the only other assembler, framework/normalize/assembler.rs and payload_normalizer.rs, is response-oriented). Wiring confirms the asymmetry: ConnectionBuffer is registered exactly once, in run_raw_ssl at main.rs:965 (comment at 964), which serves the `ssl` command via main.rs:553. The `record` command (main.rs:689-742) and `trace` command (main.rs:620-687) both dispatch to run_trace (defined main.rs:1298), whose SSL chain at main.rs:1373-1409 registers TimestampNormalizer, PayloadNormalizer, RawSecretRedactor, SSLFilter, SSEProcessor, HTTPParser, HTTPFilter and AuthHeaderRemover but never ConnectionBuffer; run_trace contains no other add_analyzer call for the SSL runner (grep shows 1373, 1378, 1383, 1387, 1392, 1399, 1403, 1407 only). PayloadNormalizer's WRITE/SEND arm (payload_normalizer.rs:104-118) removes any buffered response state and then pushes the event through untouched, and its READ/RECV buffering is strictly response reassembly; HTTPParser (http_parser.rs:231-245) parses each event independently and passes unparseable fragments straight through rather than accumulating them, so a continuation fragment is never rejoined. docs/architecture.md:182 indeed claims ConnectionBuffer covers "全管道", contradicting the wiring. The impact description is therefore supported: in the record path, a request split across SSL_write calls yields a first fragment parsed as a complete request (headers, possibly partial body) and later fragments emitted as opaque ssl events, truncating prompt/tool-call content before intent/injection analysis. I found no alternate path or generic runner hook that adds ConnectionBuffer, so the defect is real; the only caveat is that the magnitude depends on how often real clients split request bodies (documented in the module header as common), which does not refute the wiring gap.

confirmed.title: HTTPParser accepts truncated bodies as complete HTTP messages
confirmed.evidence: handle_ssl_event (http_parser.rs:223-246) parses any ssl event whose `data` merely contains HTTP markers, and parse_http_message (http_parser.rs:81-164) never checks Content-Length or chunked termination; create_http_event (http_parser.rs:167-220) sets has_body from whatever bytes arrived and records content_length only as metadata. The only guards are `partial=true` fragments from PayloadNormalizer, which never cover request writes.
confirmed.impact: A message whose body was cut across SSL_write/SSL_read events is emitted as a complete http_parser event. Downstream, routing.rs:919-922 returns empty on a serde parse error with no diagnostic, so multi-write LLM prompts vanish from intent extraction and no counter or event records the loss; detectors also run heuristics over partial prompt text.
confirmed.fix: Only emit an HTTPEvent when the message's own framing is complete (reuse normalize::message_complete/Content-Length), otherwise pass the fragment through marked undecoded so the loss is visible downstream.

verification.reason: The code says exactly what the claim says, and the path is reachable. In /tmp/mtal-audit/collector/src/framework/analyzers/http_parser.rs, handle_ssl_event (223-246) calls is_http_data (56-78, a loose marker heuristic) and then parse_http_message (81-164) at line 232-233; parse_http_message splits on CRLF, finds the blank line, and returns Some(HTTPMessage) unconditionally — it never consults Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, or the message_complete() helper that exists in framework/normalize/assembler.rs:59, so a header block plus a truncated body parses fine. create_http_event sets has_body = parsed_message.body.is_some() (188) and passes content_length only as metadata (179-182, argument at 210); HTTPEvent (event.rs:87-104) has no completeness/partial flag, so the emitted "http_parser" event is indistinguishable from a full message. The only in-parser guard is the partial=true check at 262-264, and PayloadNormalizer only sets partial for read/response framing (payload_normalizer.rs:119 → push_read, 253-256 mark_partial); WRITE/SEND events are forwarded untouched at payload_normalizer.rs:104-117, so request writes are indeed uncovered. A second, independent guard (ConnectionBuffer) exists only in run_raw_ssl (main.rs:964-965), and it too fails open for writes >= 64KB (connection_buffer.rs:199-205 pass-through) — and run_trace (main.rs:1373-1399), which builds the SSL pipeline used by the `record` command (main.rs:708 onward, ssl_http=true), omits ConnectionBuffer entirely, so raw SSL_write fragments hit HTTPParser directly. Downstream the loss is silent as claimed: routing.rs:258-266 sources body_candidate from the http_parser "body" field, extract_request_user_messages calls serde_json::from_str at 919-922 and does `Err(_) => return Vec::new()` with no diagnostic counter (the only counter nearby, DIAG_BODY_TOO_LARGE at 914-917, is for oversize bodies), while routing.rs:291-297 still runs IntentExtractor heuristics over the truncated text. The proposed fix is feasible since message_complete/framing_of are already exported from normalize/mod.rs:26. Severity high is warranted: truncation is silent, affects the primary record path, and drops multi-write LLM prompts from intent extraction.

confirmed.title: Out-of-band OpenClaw events bypass TimestampNormalizer and carry a boot-relative clock
confirmed.evidence: OpenClawRunner stamps events with monotonic_now_ns() from /proc/uptime (outofband.rs:152-166, 204-210) on the stated assumption that this matches bpf_ktime_get_ns. Every other runner is given TimestampNormalizer in run_trace (main.rs:1373, 1436, 1460, 1485), but the OpenClaw runner is added bare at main.rs:1505-1511. outofband_intent copies event.timestamp into Intent.timestamp_ns (routing.rs:967), and confidence uses intent.timestamp_ns.abs_diff(action.timestamp_ns) (correlator.rs:477).
confirmed.impact: Out-of-band intents are ~1.7e18 ns away from epoch-normalized eBPF actions, so every correlation saturates the maximum time penalty (confidence.rs:110-116) and the OutOfBandAsserted path is systematically under-scored; intents also persist timestamps that render as 1970 and break cooldown/ordering logic.
confirmed.fix: Normalize this runner's timestamps with the same boot→epoch conversion as the eBPF runners (or add TimestampNormalizer to it), and extend scripts/e2e/openclaw-outofband.sh to assert the intent timestamp falls inside the action correlation window.

verification.reason: The code says exactly what the claim cites. The OpenClaw runner stamps every event with monotonic_now_ns() (collector/src/framework/runners/outofband.rs:153 in the async stream, :95 in the test poll loop), and that helper (outofband.rs:204-210) reads the first field of /proc/uptime and returns seconds-since-boot * 1e9 — a boot-relative clock. The comment at outofband.rs:147-151 explicitly assumes this equals bpf_ktime_get_ns. In contrast, every eBPF runner is given TimestampNormalizer (main.rs:949, 1111, 1241, 1373, 1436, 1460, 1485, 1791) which converts boot ns to epoch ns (timestamp_normalizer.rs:33-45 → timestamp.rs:58-62), while the OpenClaw runner is added bare at main.rs:1511 inside the block at 1497-1516, with no add_analyzer call; its own analyzers vector is empty and AgentRunner's global chain (framework/runners/agent.rs:58-73) contains only ResponsibilityRuntime (main.rs:1687), not a normalizer. Routing special-cases source=="openclaw" (routing.rs:159) with no clock conversion and copies event.timestamp straight into Intent.timestamp_ns (routing.rs:967), which the correlator compares via abs_diff (correlator.rs:477). So the mixed-clock-domain defect is real and reachable at runtime (opt-in via MTAGENTLENS_OPENCLAW_STATE). I do downgrade severity, however: the claimed scoring impact is overstated. compute_time_penalty saturates at MAX_TIME_PENALTY = 0.05 (confidence.rs:30-36, 111-121), the L1-L3 cutoff is only 0.25 (correlator.rs:42, 51-59), and the authoritative Phase 2 batch path deliberately passes time_delta = 0 (/tmp/mtal-audit/collector/src/responsibility/evidence/correlator.rs:316-320, "batch mode: no time penalty"), so only the streaming/provisional path loses 0.05 (notably pushing L5 base 0.35 below its 0.35 cutoff). The "break cooldown" part is unsupported: the cooldown-bearing analyzers (handoff_injection.rs:116, multi_agent_anomaly.rs:693) are only attached to the SSL runner and never see OpenClaw events. The ordering/1970 part is real: intents persist the raw boot ns (writer.rs:640) and get_intents sorts by it (reader.rs:528), and live SSE serializes events through to_json_value → epoch_ns_to_epoch_ms (events.rs:60-70, server/live_sse.rs:56), yielding ~1970 timestamps; also on_action evicts boot-stamped intents with an epoch cutoff (correlator.rs:230-237, 214) and the e2e script asserts only tool_name/authority_source, not the timestamp. Net: confirmed defect, but medium rather than high.

confirmed.title: Shutdown drops the analyzer stream, orphaning eBPF children and discarding buffered state
confirmed.evidence: BinaryExecutor kills and waits for the child only after the stdout read loop completes (common.rs:310-325); kill_on_drop is never set, so dropping the stream abandons the tokio Child. On SIGINT the ResponsibilityRuntime breaks its loop and returns without draining its input (runtime.rs:2238-2248), and the raw subcommands break their select! and drop the stream at function exit (main.rs:1074-1077, 1150-1153, 1287-1290). Dropping an async_stream generator skips its tail, so payload_normalizer's flush_all (payload_normalizer.rs:380) and SSEProcessor accumulators never flush.
confirmed.impact: Ctrl+C/SIGTERM leaves root-privileged tls_capture/process/stdiocap children running with their uprobes attached while the extracted temporary binary is unlinked, and buffered responses/incomplete SSE streams are silently lost — so the 'graceful shutdown' path both leaks processes across runs and truncates the recorded dataset.
confirmed.fix: Own each child via a guard with kill_on_drop or a Drop impl, stop the child before shutdown, and drain the stream to EOF (or explicitly finalize each stateful analyzer) instead of dropping it.

verification.reason: I could not refute the core claim. In /tmp/mtal-audit/collector/src/framework/runners/common.rs, `get_json_stream` spawns the child at line 184 with no `kill_on_drop` anywhere in `collector/src` (grep returned zero hits), moves the `Child` into the `async_stream::stream!` body, and only kills/waits at lines 312-325 — i.e. strictly after the stdout read loop reaches EOF or an I/O error; the stream has no cancellation arm and no Drop guard, so dropping the generator simply drops the `tokio::process::Child` without killing it (tokio's default). The drop path is genuinely reached on shutdown: `setup_signal_handler` (main.rs:51-77) only stores `SHUTDOWN_REQUESTED`/`RUNTIME_SHUTDOWN` and prints metrics, while the consumer loops in main.rs:1064-1081, 1140-1157, 1277-1294 and 1717-1734 (the main `trace` path) `break` on `shutdown_requested()` and return `Ok(())`, dropping the stream; `AgentRunner::run` (runners/agent.rs:50-77) holds the runner streams in `select_all`, so they die with the merged stream, and `SslRunner::run` (ssl.rs:101-112) shows the `Child` is only reachable through that generator. The buffered-state loss is likewise real: `PayloadNormalizer::process` (analyzers/payload_normalizer.rs:371-383) puts `flush_all()` (line 380) after the `while let Some(event)` loop, so it runs only on normal EOF and is skipped when the generator is dropped; `ResponsibilityRuntime::process` (responsibility/runtime/runtime.rs:2237-2243) breaks on the shutdown flag without draining its remaining input, dropping all upstream generators. The only imprecision is the SSEProcessor half of the evidence: `SSEProcessor::process` (analyzers/sse_processor.rs:648+) is a `filter_map` with no end-of-stream flush at all, so its accumulators are lost on normal EOF too — dropping the stream does not uniquely skip a tail flush there — but that is a minor overstatement inside an otherwise accurate report, not a refutation. The orphaned-child impact is slightly probabilistic (a child writing to the now-closed stdout pipe may die of SIGPIPE, and `_temp_dir`/TempDir drop only unlinks the already-exec'd binary), but for root-privileged eBPF capture binaries that sit idle waiting for probes, non-kill is the default and the leak across runs stands.

confirmed.title: Capture read errors are converted into a clean end-of-stream
confirmed.evidence: In BinaryExecutor::get_json_stream, any non-Interrupted read error logs a warning and breaks out of the generator loop (common.rs:298-306). The generator then performs its normal kill/wait tail and ends; get_json_stream already returned Ok, so Runner::run, AgentRunner and main see a normal EOF and exit 0. There is no terminal diagnostic event and no capture-health counter in the event stream.
confirmed.impact: A capture that dies mid-run (child crash, EIO, permission revocation) produces a log/DB that looks like a complete, valid run; offline evaluation cannot distinguish an aborted trace from a finished one.
confirmed.fix: Emit a terminal diagnostic event (or a stream error surfaced through the runner result) carrying the io::Error and make the CLI exit non-zero / record capture-health on abnormal termination.

verification.reason: I checked the cited region verbatim. common.rs:282-307 is the read loop: Ok(None) (EOF) breaks at 290-292, Interrupted retries at 294-296, and every other Err logs only a warn at 299-304 and breaks at 305 — the error value is discarded, nothing is yielded. The stream type is fixed at common.rs:13 (`JsonStream = Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = serde_json::Value> + Send>>`), so the error cannot be surfaced as an item, and get_json_stream returns `Ok(Box::pin(stream))` unconditionally at line 328 after the loop. The tail at 310-325 unconditionally kills and waits for the child, with exit status logged only at debug (line 320); a non-zero child status is never inspected or returned. Callers confirm normal-EOF semantics: process.rs:103-110, ssl.rs:103-110 and stdio.rs:133-141 just `map`/`filter_map` the Value stream and return Ok; AgentRunner merges via select_all (agent.rs:51-70), and main.rs:1712-1731 consumes until `None => break` then returns `Ok(())`, so the process exits 0. I found no capture-health counter, truncation flag on the run, or terminal diagnostic event anywhere in collector/src (grep for capture-health/incomplete/truncated/exit_status yields only payload-decode diagnostics in payload_normalizer and normalize/*, unrelated to process read failures). The working-tree copy is byte-identical to the snapshot (diff empty), so this is not stale. One imprecision that does not refute the finding: the "child crash" example in the impact would actually terminate via EOF (Ok(None) at line 290) rather than this Err branch — but that path is equally silent and only strengthens the underlying defect (abnormal termination indistinguishable from a completed run). The medium severity is appropriate: read errors are rare, but offline evaluation cannot currently distinguish an aborted capture from a finished one.

confirmed.title: Payloads marked truncated/lossy are finalized as complete SSE and HTTP messages
confirmed.evidence: tls_capture marks lost bytes with truncated/bytes_lost (bpftools/include/payload_json.h:40), and PayloadNormalizer propagates this as `"truncated": status != "ok"` plus decode_status (payload_normalizer.rs:500-510). SSEProcessor checks only the `partial` flag (sse_processor.rs:671-676) and then parses `data` unconditionally (sse_processor.rs:703-712); HTTPParser likewise only checks `partial` (http_parser.rs:258-264). Only an optional SSLFilter expression can observe `truncated`.
confirmed.impact: A response that lost bytes in the ring buffer is merged into a 'complete' sse_processor/http_parser event and fed to the detectors; missing model output is indistinguishable from output that was never produced, biasing false negatives and invalidating completeness claims about the dataset.
confirmed.fix: Inherit the truncation flag into merged/parsed events, mark them lossy, and emit a decode diagnostic instead of a normal completed event.

verification.reason: The cited behavior is real. bpftools/include/payload_json.h:39-42 emits `"truncated":true,"bytes_lost":N` when buf_size < declared_len; collector/src/framework/normalize/transport.rs:231-234 parses it into WirePayload.truncated; payload_normalizer.rs:201 accumulates it into conn.truncated, and payload_normalizer.rs:278-281 emits the completed synthetic message with status "lossy" and (via synthetic_event at payload_normalizer.rs:507-508) `"truncated": status != "ok"` plus decode_status. That synthetic event is source "ssl", has no `partial` flag, and is pushed straight downstream (normalizer runs before the parsers per main.rs:949-982). SSEProcessor's only lossiness guard is the `partial` check at sse_processor.rs:669-671; it then reads `data` at 704-707, calls is_sse_data at 710, parses SSE in 714-715 and can finalize a merged event, with no inspection of `truncated` or `decode_status` anywhere in the file (grep for both returns nothing). HTTPParser likewise only checks `partial` at http_parser.rs:258-264 and then parses in handle_ssl_event (230-244), with no truncated/lossy check. The merged SSEProcessorEvent (event.rs:11-26) and HTTPEvent (event.rs:87-105) have no truncated/decode_status field and to_event serializes the struct only (event.rs:64-69, 149-160), so the lossiness marker is dropped at exactly the point the "complete" event is created; FileLogger runs after SSEProcessor (main.rs:1038), so even the log loses it. The only consumer of `truncated` is SSLFilter (ssl_filter.rs:269-275), an optional user expression, as claimed. The claim's line citations are off by a couple of lines (the partial guard is 669-671, data extraction 704-707) but they point at the right code. Caveat on reachability: in the common single-response case missing bytes usually make message_complete return Ok(None) or an error (assembler.rs:59-73), yielding an "incomplete"/"malformed" diagnostic whose fragments are marked partial and correctly skipped; a lossy *completed* event requires the truncated stream to re-frame successfully (e.g., pipelined/over-consumed content-length or coincidental chunk re-sync), so occurrence is rare. Still, the code explicitly constructs the "lossy" completed path and no stage rejects or propagates it, so the defect stands.

confirmed.title: System metrics rely on hardcoded 4 KiB pages and USER_HZ=100
confirmed.evidence: get_process_memory multiplies /proc/<pid>/statm page counts by `let page_size = 4u64;` (system.rs:421), and calculate_cpu_percentage divides clock ticks by `let user_hz = 100.0;` (system.rs:462). Neither value is read from the kernel. RSS/VSZ in the emitted payload (system.rs:345-350) feeds MultiAgentAnomaly's 2048 MB memory-storm test (multi_agent_anomaly.rs:595-603) and cpu.percent feeds its 92% CPU test (multi_agent_anomaly.rs:585-593).
confirmed.impact: On aarch64/ppc64 kernels with 64 KiB pages RSS and VSZ are under-reported 16x, so sustained_high_memory requires 32 GB of real usage; on kernels where CLK_TCK is not 100 the CPU percentage is scaled wrong. Both are published as resource measurements and used for alerting.
confirmed.fix: Read page size and CLK_TCK via libc::sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE/_SC_CLK_TCK) once at startup and use them in both calculations.

verification.reason: The cited code is exactly as claimed. In /tmp/mtal-audit/collector/src/framework/runners/system.rs, get_process_memory reads /proc/<pid>/statm at line 413, and line 421 hardcodes `let page_size = 4u64;`, then line 425 multiplies both the RSS and VSZ page counts by it; calculate_cpu_percentage at line 462 hardcodes `let user_hz = 100.0;` and line 464 divides tick deltas by it. There is no sysconf/_SC_PAGESIZE/_SC_CLK_TCK/libc page-size probe anywhere in the collector (grep across collector/src found only these two constants), and no alternate RSS source: the only value flows are total_rss_kb/total_vsz_kb at lines 285-310 into the payload at lines 345-350, which is consumed by multi_agent_anomaly.rs at lines 578-597 (`rss_mb >= 2048`) and lines 575-586 (`percent >= 92.0`). The impact is real for 64 KiB-page Linux kernels (aarch64/ppc64), where statm pages are 64 KiB and RSS/VSZ are under-reported 16x, making the 2048 MB memory-storm alert require ~32 GB; the USER_HZ=100 assumption is additionally wrong on architectures whose userspace CLK_TCK differs (e.g., alpha's 1024), so the CPU percentage is mis-scaled there. The only mitigating factor is that mainstream x86_64 and most aarch64 kernels use 4 KiB pages and USER_HZ=100, so this does not fire on typical hosts, but it is a genuine portability/correctness defect in published resource measurements used for alerting, so medium severity stands.

confirmed.title: FILE_OPEN writes are counted as reads by both propagation analyzers
confirmed.evidence: detect_from_process records every process FILE_OPEN into recent_file_reads and shared_file_readers without inspecting flags (handoff_injection.rs:236-268); multi_agent_anomaly.rs:410-428 does the same. The wire event does carry the openat flags (bpftools/process/process_json.h:44-47, process.bpf.c:326), so read/write is distinguishable. The 3-agent propagation threshold is at handoff_injection.rs:247-250.
confirmed.impact: The agent that writes a poisoned shared artifact is itself recorded as a reader, so a propagation chain of length 3 can be produced by two real readers; 'file reads' in the acceptance logic include O_WRONLY/O_RDWR creates, inflating cross-agent propagation alerts and skewing any measured precision.
confirmed.fix: Classify the open from flags (O_WRONLY/O_RDWR/O_CREAT ⇒ write) and record only reads as reads, reusing one shared classifier instead of duplicating the logic in two analyzers.

verification.reason: Confirmed in the snapshot. handoff_injection.rs:236-268 handles event_name == "FILE_OPEN" by calling state.record_file_read (line 239) for every open and record_shared_file_reader (lines 242-243) for every fixture-path opener, with no read of event.data["flags"]; record_file_read (line 87) and record_shared_file_reader (line 99) do no access-mode classification. The propagation gate is chain.len() >= 3 at lines 247-250, and propagation_chain (line 109) returns the raw opener set, so a writer consumes one of the three slots. multi_agent_anomaly.rs:410-428 is identical: line 413 queues every open as a read, lines 422-428 add every opener to shared_file_readers, and detect_team_causal_propagation (lines 535-546) gates on readers.len() < 3 without flags. Read/write is distinguishable on the wire: process_json.h:47 prints "flags":%d, process.bpf.c:326 and :388 copy the openat flags, is_file_open_noise (process.bpf.c:47-95) and should_report_file_ops (process.c:721) filter only path/PID, and process.c:714-743 emits write opens as FILE_OPEN; no collector-side filter drops write opens before these analyzers (the only flag consumers are file_access_audit.rs:305 and responsibility/evidence/action_classifier.rs:16-131, which already classify write flags, so the proposed shared classifier is feasible). The writer-is-a-reader effect also feeds detect_acceptance (handoff_injection.rs:342-356) and detect_shared_artifact_acceptance (multi_agent_anomaly.rs:493-505), so both propagation and acceptance alerts are inflated as claimed. Minor nuance not a refutation: hash_file_open (process.c:247-258) dedupes on pid+path without flags, so same-process write/read pairs may collapse, but that does not prevent a distinct writer agent from being counted as a reader.

confirmed.title: StageMetrics has no producer; /health and /ready are permanently degraded
confirmed.evidence: The only production construction is WebServer::with_channels(event_sender, log_file, alert_tx, None) at main.rs:1869; with_health_state has no caller. No code ever constructs StageMetrics (pipeline_contract.rs:209) or updates HealthState, and `ready` is only ever read (web.rs:1721), never set true. When health_state is None, serve_health returns HealthStatus::Degraded with an explicit 'no StageMetrics producer is wired' warning (web.rs:1801-1813) and serve_ready returns 503 (web.rs:1717-1735).
confirmed.impact: /health never reports healthy and /ready never reports ready for any orchestrator, and the framework's pipeline-contract module exists only as types — documented health/readiness behavior is not implemented.
confirmed.fix: Wire a StageMetrics registry that analyzers/runners update and pass an Arc<Mutex<HealthState>> to WebServer (setting ready on first processed event), or delete the endpoints/types and document that they are unsupported.

verification.reason: The claim is accurate and I could not refute it. The only production construction of WebServer is `WebServer::with_channels(event_sender, log_file, alert_tx, None)` at collector/src/main.rs:1869, which passes `None` for health_state; `with_health_state` exists only as its own definition at collector/src/server/web.rs:102-107 with zero callers, and `HealthState::new` (web.rs:43-49) also has zero callers across the entire snapshot (grep for `HealthState`, `HealthState::new`, and `stage_metrics` over all files, not just *.rs, returned only the declarations/usages in web.rs and api_types.rs). `StageMetrics` is declared at collector/src/framework/analyzers/pipeline_contract.rs:606 but is never constructed anywhere (`StageMetrics {`, `StageMetrics::default`, and `StageMetrics::new` all have no hits), so `HealthState.stage_metrics` can never be populated. `ready` is initialized `false` at web.rs:48 and only ever read (`guard.ready` at web.rs:1721); there is no assignment of `true` anywhere. The None path is genuinely reached: `start()` clones `self.health_state` (web.rs:129) and forwards it through `handle_request` (web.rs:192), the routes at web.rs:286-293 dispatch `/health` to `serve_health` and `/ready` to `serve_ready`, and `start_web_server_if_enabled` is invoked by the production subcommand paths in main.rs (e.g., lines 1049, 1124, 1259, 1702, 1806). Consequently `serve_ready`'s None branch returns HTTP 503 with `"no StageMetrics producer is wired"` (web.rs:1717-1735), and `serve_health`'s None branch returns `HealthStatus::Degraded` with the same warning and an empty stages map (web.rs:1801-1813), not merely a doc-comment claim. The behavior is deliberately honest rather than fabricated-healthy (and is even noted in docs/evaluation/mechanism-audit-2026-10-20-v2.md:133), but the underlying producer is absent, so the endpoint behavior is permanently degraded exactly as alleged and the pipeline-contract metrics module is types-only. Severity stays medium: any orchestrator using /ready would never see the service become ready and /health can never report healthy, but the response is explicit and safe (no false-positive readiness), limiting blast radius.

confirmed.title: FileAccessAudit misclassifies O_PATH and O_TMPFILE opens
confirmed.evidence: classify_access_type treats `flags & 0x400000` as O_PATH (file_access_audit.rs:169-172). On Linux O_PATH is 0x200000 and 0x400000 is __O_TMPFILE (O_DIRECTORY 0x10000 in the next branch is correct). Files opened with O_PATH therefore fall through to the default Read classification, while O_TMPFILE creates are classified Execute.
confirmed.impact: access_type, risk_level and the emitted audit event are wrong for those opens, so the file-access audit can miss anonymous-file creation and mislabel descriptor-only opens.
confirmed.fix: Use libc::O_PATH / libc::O_TMPFILE (or the documented constants) instead of numeric literals, with a table test covering each flag.

verification.reason: The core constant mismatch is real and reachable. In /tmp/mtal-audit/collector/src/framework/analyzers/file_access_audit.rs, classify_access_type (lines 163-186) checks flags & 0x1/0x2 for Write first (165-167), then `flags & 0x400000` for "O_PATH" at 170-171, then `flags & 0x10000` for O_DIRECTORY at 175-176. System headers confirm O_PATH = 010000000 = 0x200000 and __O_TMPFILE = 020000000 = 0x400000 (O_TMPFILE = 0x410000 on x86_64), so the 0x400000 test is not O_PATH. The flags are genuine raw openat flags: bpftools/process/process.bpf.c:289/326 copies ctx->args[2] into file_op.flags, process_json.h:47 emits it, and file_access_audit.rs:305 reads event.data["flags"], so a standalone O_PATH open (0x200000, e.g. O_PATH|O_CLOEXEC = 0x280000) matches no branch and falls through to Read at 185, while O_PATH|O_DIRECTORY lands in Stat at 176. The analyzer is live (collector/src/main.rs:1633), and there is no test covering these flags. However, two parts of the stated impact are refuted: (1) successful O_TMPFILE creates can never be classified Execute, because the kernel requires O_WRONLY/O_RDWR with O_TMPFILE (O_RDONLY|O_TMPFILE returns EINVAL), so lines 165-167 return Write before line 170 — only a failing EINVAL syscall recorded at sys_enter would reach the Execute branch, so "miss anonymous-file creation" is false; and (2) risk_level is unaffected, since classify_risk (222-250) special-cases only Write and otherwise keys on the workspace boundary, so Execute vs Read yields the same level (low inside, medium outside). No other code consumes access_type (grep outside this analyzer/contract found none), so the practical effect is confined to the emitted "access_type" string at line 343. The defect is real but narrower than claimed, so low severity is appropriate.

confirmed.title: massive_file_scan evidence reads a field FILE_OPEN never emits
confirmed.evidence: The massive_file_scan alert is built from a FILE_OPEN event but reads `event.data.get("filename")` (multi_agent_anomaly.rs:450). process_json.h emits `filepath` for FILE_OPEN events (bpftools/process/process_json.h:44-47); `filename` exists only on EXEC events (bpftools/process/process.c:660).
confirmed.impact: The alert's evidence field is always null, so a consumer cannot tell which file triggered the scan alert; the same analyzer reads `filepath` correctly elsewhere (multi_agent_anomaly.rs:411).
confirmed.fix: Read `filepath` for FILE_OPEN alerts and keep `filename` for EXEC alerts.

verification.reason: Line 450 does literally read `event.data.get("filename")` for the `massive_file_scan` alert, and no event that can reach that branch carries a `filename` field. One correction to the claim: line 450 is not in the direct FILE_OPEN arm — that arm starts at line 409 and correctly reads `filepath` (line 411). Line 450 sits inside the `"SUMMARY"` arm (line 262), where `summary_type` comes from `event.data["type"]` (lines 263-267). The only in-repo SUMMARY emitter, `bpftools/process_ext/map_flush.h:106-119` (`print_summary_json`), emits timestamp/event/comm/pid/type/detail/count/total_bytes/extra — the path lives in `detail`, not `filename` or `filepath`. The live producer's FILE_OPEN JSON (`bpftools/process_json.h:44-45`) emits `filepath`, and `filename` appears only in EXEC emissions (`bpftools/process.c:660` and `:681`). The process runner passes the parsed JSON through untouched as `Event.data` (`collector/src/framework/runners/process.rs:92-95`), and `build_anomaly_event` (multi_agent_anomaly.rs:749-778) only copies the event name into `source_event`, so nothing enriches the alert with the path later. Hence the evidence is always null. Two caveats that do not refute the defect: (1) the proposed fix is mis-targeted — for this SUMMARY-path alert the correct source field is `detail`, not `filepath`; (2) `process_new.h` labels the map_flush aggregation path dormant, and no live code emits SUMMARY `type=FILE_OPEN`, so this branch appears unreachable in production, which keeps severity low rather than raising it.

confirmed.title: Event::to_json and Event::from_json disagree on timestamp units
confirmed.evidence: to_json_value writes `timestamp` as epoch milliseconds plus `timestamp_ns` in nanoseconds (events.rs:64-76), while from_json deserializes the derived `timestamp` field (documented and used internally as nanoseconds) and ignores `timestamp_ns` (events.rs:90-93). The derived Serialize used by serde_json::to_string(&event) (ssl.rs:229, process.rs:247) writes the same `timestamp` key in nanoseconds, a second public representation with a different unit. from_json has no production caller.
confirmed.impact: Any round-trip from_json(to_json(e)) puts a millisecond value into a nanosecond field (a 1e6 error), and the two serialization APIs produce incompatible JSON for the same event; currently latent but easy to hit for external consumers.
confirmed.fix: Make from_json read timestamp_ns (falling back to timestamp × 1e6), or remove from_json/Deserialize if unused, and make the serde representation of Event explicit so only one unit is ever emitted per key.

The derived-serde sites named in the evidence do exist and are reachable (ssl.rs:229 and process.rs:247 both serde_json::to_string(&event)), emitting a nanosecond "timestamp" under the same key that to_json_value uses for milliseconds, so the two public representations are genuinely incompatible. confirmed.title: FPR bootstrap interval is 0.0 by construction because benign outcomes are never encoded

confirmed.title: Offline dimension ablation reuses a fusion formula the collector no longer executes

confirmed.title: Repro manifest records git_dirty=true for every run
confirmed.evidence: scripts/repro.sh:51-55 `version()` returns `stdout.splitlines()[0]`; on a clean tree `git status --porcelain` prints nothing, causing IndexError and returning the truthy string "unavailable". Line 60 then computes `"git_dirty": bool(version(["git", "status", "--porcelain"]))`, which is True for both clean and dirty trees.
confirmed.impact: The artifact provenance manifest cannot distinguish a clean-tree build from a dirty one, defeating its purpose as reproducibility evidence.
confirmed.fix: Treat empty stdout as False (return "" or call `git status --porcelain` directly and compare with "").

verification.reason: The claim reproduces exactly. In /tmp/mtal-audit/scripts/repro.sh, `version()` at lines 51-55 does `subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.splitlines()[0]` and returns the string `"unavailable"` on `IndexError`/`OSError`. `git status --porcelain` emits zero bytes on a clean tree, so `"".splitlines()` is `[]`, `[][0]` raises `IndexError`, and `"unavailable"` is a non-empty (truthy) string. Line 60 then computes `"git_dirty": bool(version(["git", "status", "--porcelain"]))`, which is `True` on a clean tree; on a dirty tree the actual porcelain text is returned and is likewise truthy, and if git is absent the `OSError` branch again yields `"unavailable"` → `True`. I verified the semantics in an isolated interpreter: `version('')` returns `'unavailable'` and `bool(...)` is `True`. Line 60 is unconditional inside the manifest payload dict (lines 57-78) executed by the step at lines 37-38, and line 79 writes it verbatim, with no downstream normalization — a grep of the snapshot shows no other code rewriting this manifest. The parallel helpers elsewhere (e.g. compare/scripts/audit/audit_submission_package.py:615-619, which returns `""`) are not used here and do not mask the bug. So the field is constant-True and cannot distinguish clean from dirty builds, exactly as claimed; severity medium is appropriate since this is artifact reproducibility provenance, not runtime behavior.

Line 176 is `@cd $(COLLECTOR_DIR) && cargo fmt`; line 177 is exactly `@cd $(FRONTEND_DIR) && npx prettier --write 'src/**/*.{ts,tsx,css}' 2>/dev/null || true`; line 178 prints the success message "代码格式化完成". FRONTEND_DIR is defined as `frontend` at line 27, and /tmp/mtal-audit/frontend contains app/, components/, lib/, engine/, types/, etc. but no src/ directory (`ls /tmp/mtal-audit/frontend/src` fails with ENOENT). Running the same npx prettier command in frontend reproduces `[error] No files matching the pattern were found: "src/**/*.{ts,tsx,css}"`, and because stderr is redirected to /dev/null and the whole compound is terminated with `|| true`, the nonzero exit and error text are both discarded, so `make fmt` reports success after formatting zero frontend files. Nothing else in the reached path compensates: the other frontend targets wired in the Makefile are test (151), build (156), lint (172, which runs only `npm run lint && npm run type-check`, not `format:check`), and install/dev/build; there is no other prettier invocation or fmt-check target anywhere in the Makefile, and the snapshot has no .github/workflows directory to run `format:check` either. One minor citation slip in the evidence: the frontend `format` script is at frontend/package.json line 9 (`"format": "prettier --write ."`), with `format:check` at line 10 and `type-check` at line 11, not line 11 for `format`; this is an off-by-two in the line reference only and does not affect the defect, which is fully reproducible. The suggested fix (delegate to `npm run format` and let the exit status propagate) is correct.

confirmed.title: Kernel floor still documented as 4.1+ in two places capabilities.json says were fixed
confirmed.evidence: CLAUDE.md:332 describes the eBPF kernel matrix as "4.1+ / 5.0+ / 5.8+" and bpftools/README.md:568 states "Requires Linux kernel with eBPF support (4.1+)". docs/capabilities.json:9-13 sets the minimum to 5.8 because all three programs use BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF, and its note says those 4.1+ claims were to be corrected; the 5.8 floor is implemented in collector/src/doctor.rs:74,136.
